# The Ten-Minute Heron

The great blue heron stands in the shallows of a retention pond behind an office park, and I stop because it seems to ask me to. This is not beauty that announces itself. The pond is ringed with grass gone to seed and a crust of goose droppings; beyond it, an empty parking lot throws back the morning light like a held breath. But the bird—gray as a curtain, still as a fact—has a way of standing that makes everything around it look hurried. It is taller than it first appeared. Its neck is folded like a carpenter's rule. One yellow eye regards the water with what I can only describe as professional interest, and its reflection hangs below it in the pond, doubled and upside down, so that there are two herons balanced head to head like a paper fold.

I stand at the edge of the mown strip and watch. For a long time nothing happens, and I mean that literally: nothing happens. The heron moves only in increments so small they might be imagined—a slow telescoping of the neck, weight shifted from one yellow foot to the other. Under the surface, small fish drift like commas. My mind wanders to the things I'm supposed to be doing today, and I bring it back the way you'd retrieve a dog off a neighbor's lawn. Then the neck uncoils all at once, faster than I can properly follow, and the beak is in the water, and when it comes up there is a fish folding in it, silver against gray, and the bird tips its head back and the fish is gone.

I check my watch, out of curiosity rather than boredom. Ten minutes. It felt like twenty-five, or like nothing at all—the two experiences braided together, the way ten minutes of held attention can both vanish and outlast itself.

William James wrote in 1890 that "my experience is what I agree to attend to." He meant it as a psychologist's claim about how consciousness is built, but I've come to think it is closer to an arithmetic of a life. What else is a life? Not the dates on a stone. A life is the sum of what was actually noticed—the felt minutes, the ones someone was home for. Attention, on this view, is not a resource we spend, despite how we talk about spending it. It is the medium we exist in, the water the heron and I are both standing in. Less like currency, more like air. The question of what you attend to is not, finally, a productivity question. It is the question of what you are.

The ten minutes went long, I think, for the same reason childhood summers went long. The obvious explanation is proportional: a summer is a tenth of a ten-year-old's life and a fiftieth of a fifty-year-old's, so of course it shrinks. But the better explanation is about density. A child's summer is stuffed with firsts—first firefly, first dive off the high board, first thunderstorm watched from a porch—and novelty forces the mind to record. Psychologists sometimes call this the holiday paradox: a week somewhere new flies by in the moment, then feels enormous in memory, because so much of it got written down; a month of routine does the opposite, dragging in the moment and vanishing in retrospect. Felt time is a function of what gets noticed. The heron's ten minutes were partly firsts—there had never been those exact ten minutes before, and the bird was an event my brain refused to summarize—so they were recorded, not skimmed. They exist.

Here is what I wish someone had told me earlier: attention has a knowledge requirement. You cannot attend to what you cannot distinguish. For years the dawn chorus was, to me, a single bright texture, lovely and undifferentiated, the sound of the word "birds." Then I learned five or six songs, and the same dawn broke apart into individuals. The cardinal says birdie-birdie-birdie, slurred at the edges. The Carolina wren insists on tea-kettle, tea-kettle, tea-kettle with a fluency that ought to embarrass a bird that size. The song sparrow drops a few bright chips and falls into a stuttering trill. The birds did not change. The resolution changed. The world's grain was always this fine; I simply hadn't been taught to feel it.

And this scales upward without limit. It's said of the old Japanese chicken-sexers that they could sort day-old chicks at a glance, separating males from females by a pattern they could not articulate—decades of looking had built perception where the rest of us have a shrug. Radiologists who read thousands of scans develop gaze patterns amateurs don't have; the nodule announces itself to a trained sweep of attention and hides from an untrained one. A perfumer, a sommelier, a proofreader, a bird dog: in every case what looks like superior attention turns out, underneath, to be superior distinction. Learning is the sandpaper. Which I find hopeful, because it means attention is not a talent doled out at birth but a practice with a curriculum—there is always more world available to a person who has learned one more name.
